record.paper_title: Protocols for Observational Studies: Methods and Open Problems
record.context_brief: Evidence assessment for elaborate causal theories
record.original_question: An elaborate theory for an observational study protocol is a prespecified set of multiple predictions about how the data should look if a treatment has a causal effect. Ordered testing can prioritize the primary prediction and control the familywise Type I error rate across multiple tested predictions, but it may give limited information about lower-priority aspects of the theory. What statistical methods can assess the evidence for such an elaborate theory, including both individual predicted aspects and the fraction of the theory that is corroborated, while retaining valid multiplicity control and the prespecified priority among predictions?

evidence.quote: An elaborate theory is a set of multiple predictions about how the data would look if the treatment has an effect. In Fisher’s advice to use elaborate theories, one needs to make the predictions about how a treatment effect would manifest before seeing the data.

Although ordered testing of an elaborate theory has considerable advantages, one negative aspect is that although one might want to put a higher priority on certain aspects of the theory, one might want some information on all aspects. A different approach to assessing the evidence for an elaborate theory is to make inferences about the fraction of the elaborate theory that is corroborated as well as individual aspects of the theory. Further research on ways to assess the evidence for an elaborate theory would be useful.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider an observational study designed to test a causal hypothesis that a treatment T has an effect on an outcome. Prior to examining the data, the investigator specifies an "elaborate theory" consisting of an ordered list of K predictions P_1, P_2, ..., P_K (with P_1 highest priority) about empirical patterns that should appear in the data if T truly causes the outcome. Each prediction P_k corresponds to a testable null hypothesis H_k stating that the prediction does not hold (e.g., absence of a dose-response trend, absence of a specified subgroup contrast, absence of a predicted comparison-group difference, etc.). The investigator wants:

(a) Valid familywise Type I error control: P(reject any true H_k) ≤ α under the global null that the treatment has no causal effect, and more generally strong familywise error control across {H_1,...,H_K}.
(b) Respect for the prespecified priority: the procedure should preserve the special status of H_1 (e.g., always test H_1 first at level α, and allow further tests only conditionally), in the spirit of fixed-sequence/ordered testing.
(c) Information about every prediction, not only the top-priority one: in particular, inference (with simultaneous validity) about which individual predictions P_k are corroborated.
(d) Inference about the "fraction of the theory corroborated," i.e., a simultaneously valid lower confidence bound L(α) such that, with probability ≥ 1-α, at least L(α) out of the K predictions hold (equivalently, simultaneous confidence statements on the number of false null hypotheses among H_1,...,H_K).

Problem. Construct a multiple-testing procedure, together with an accompanying confidence statement on the number of corroborated predictions, that simultaneously satisfies (a)–(d). More precisely, design a procedure Φ producing (i) a rejection set R ⊆ {1,...,K} controlling the familywise error rate at level α in the strong sense, (ii) preserving the prespecified ordering in the sense that whenever R is nonempty, hypothesis H_1 is rejected (or more generally, the procedure reduces to a chosen ordered-testing procedure on the top-priority hypothesis), and (iii) yielding a (1-α)-simultaneous lower confidence bound on Σ_k 1{H_k is false}. Establish its validity and characterize its power relative to the standard ordered (fixed-sequence) testing procedure.
artifact.status_search_result: The question, as posed, is an open methodological research direction: existing approaches include ordered/fixed-sequence testing (Rosenbaum), closed testing with weighting, and simultaneous lower bounds on the number of false hypotheses (Goeman–Solari, Genovese–Wasserman). However, no canonical method jointly delivers strict ordered priority, strong FWER control, and a simultaneous bound on the fraction of corroborated predictions for elaborate-theory observational-study protocols. The matter is explicitly flagged as needing further research and no definitive solution is established in the literature surveyed.

status_evidence.title: Goeman & Solari, Multiple testing for exploratory research
status_evidence.snippet: Provides simultaneous lower confidence bounds on the number of true discoveries among any subset of hypotheses.
status_evidence.claim: General machinery exists for simultaneous bounds on fraction of true effects, but not specialized to ordered elaborate-theory protocols.

status_evidence.title: Rosenbaum, Observational Studies and elaborate theories
status_evidence.snippet: Discussion of Fisher's elaborate-theories advice and ordered testing in observational study design.
status_evidence.claim: Ordered testing is standard but does not directly produce inference on the fraction of corroborated predictions.
